q-300758.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(-2{x}^{4})}{(-\frac{8}{{x}^{6}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{10}}{4} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{1}{4}\cdot {x}^{10}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{10}\end{aligned}

q-35612.name: Question 3
q-35612.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the powers and multiply the two functions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }({p}^{3}(x)\cdot {q}^{2}(x)) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({(p(x))}^{3}\cdot {(q(x))}^{2}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({(-3{x}^{3})}^{3}\cdot {(-3{x}^{3})}^{2}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(-27{x}^{9}\cdot 9{x}^{6}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }((-27\cdot 9){x}^{9+6}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(-243\cdot {x}^{15}) \\  & =-243\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{15}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{15}$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{15}=\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the negative constant $-243$ changes the sign of the limit. 
So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & =-243\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{15} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{15} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }(-243{x}^{15})=-\infty .
$$

q-99289.name: Question 4
q-99289.problem: Given that $p(x)=3{x}^{2}$ and $q(x)=5{x}^{7},$ what is ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }(p(x)\cdot q(x))?$
q-99289.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the two functions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(p(x)\cdot q(x)) & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(3{x}^{2}\cdot 5{x}^{7}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }((3\cdot 5){x}^{2+7}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(15\cdot {x}^{9}) \\  & =15\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{9}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{9}$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{9}=-\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $15$ does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}15\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{9}={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{9}=-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(15{x}^{9})=-\infty .
$$

15

−8

∞

−∞

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we multiply the two functions, as follows: limx→−∞(p(x)⋅q(x))=limx→−∞(3x2⋅5x7)=limx→−∞((3⋅5)x2+7)=limx→−∞(15⋅x9)=15⋅limx→−∞x9

The graph y=x9 is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that limx→−∞x9=−∞.

Multiplication by the positive constant 15 does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have 15⋅limx→−∞x9=limx→−∞x9=−∞.

Therefore, we conclude that limx→−∞(15x9)=−∞.

q-99294.name: Question 5
q-99294.problem: Given that $p(x)=6{x}^{9}$ and $q(x)=15{x}^{7},$ what is ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}\cdot q(x)}{p(x)}?$
q-99294.worked_solution:
First, let's calculate ${x}^{2}\cdot q(x):$

$$
{x}^{2}\cdot q(x)={x}^{2}\cdot (15{x}^{7})=15{x}^{9}
$$

When we divide the two functions ${x}^{2}\cdot q(x)$ and $p(x),$ we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}\cdot q(x)}{p(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{15{x}^{9}}{6{x}^{9}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{15}{6} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
